questions.question: On the IBM 360/91, a floating-point add issues while an earlier multiply still runs: the add waits in a station watching a common results bus and fires the moment its operands are broadcast. Which scheduling algorithm makes this possible?
questions.explanation: Tomasulo's algorithm uses reservation stations and a common data bus (CDB) with register tags to schedule instructions dynamically out of order, eliminating name dependences via implicit renaming.

questions.question: In a Tomasulo machine, an ADD whose second operand is still pending waits in a small per-functional-unit buffer holding the operand's tag until the common data bus delivers it. What is that buffer called?
questions.explanation: Reservation stations sit before each functional unit, storing the instruction plus operand values/tags; they free the instruction to execute the moment its operands broadcast on the CDB.

questions.question: A store finishes early in an out-of-order core, but its result must not become permanent until all older instructions have committed — a pending branch misprediction could still squash it. Which structure queues results for in-order commit?
questions.explanation: The ROB holds speculative results in program order and retires them from the head only when safe, giving precise exceptions and correct state despite out-of-order execution.

questions.question: A CDC 6600-style control unit keeps a status entry per register recording which functional unit will write it, stalling issue only when an instruction would hit a real WAW or RAW conflict. What is this mechanism?
questions.explanation: A scoreboard tracks pending writers per register and per functional unit, issuing instructions when their operands are safe — the ancestor of Tomasulo-style dynamic scheduling.

questions.question: At fetch time — before a branch is even decoded — the CPU looks up its PC in a small cache holding recently seen 'branch PC -> target PC' pairs so the next fetch can go straight to the predicted target. What is this structure?
questions.explanation: The BTB supplies the taken target during fetch, hiding the fact that the branch isn't decoded until later; a direction predictor decides taken/not-taken while the BTB supplies where to.

questions.question: A branch predictor keeps a shift register of the last several outcomes of all branches (global history) and uses it to index a table of 2-bit saturating counters, capturing correlations between different branches. What predictor family is this?
questions.explanation: Two-level (correlating) predictors use history — local per-branch or global — to select a pattern-history-table entry holding a 2-bit counter, exploiting branch-to-branch correlation.

questions.question: Two nearby instructions both write architectural register x6 for unrelated reasons, which would force a WAW stall; instead the hardware maps each destination to a different physical register and both proceed. What technique is this?
questions.explanation: Register renaming assigns each architectural destination a fresh physical register, eliminating WAW and WAR (anti-/output) dependences so only true RAW chains constrain execution.

questions.question: A compiler rewrites a four-iteration loop as four inline copies of the body, deleting three compare-and-branch sequences and exposing more independent instructions to the scheduler. What transformation is this?
questions.explanation: Loop unrolling replicates the loop body and removes per-iteration control overhead, enlarging the basic block so more ILP is visible to the pipeline.

questions.question: While the front end executes a long sequential code region, a next-line engine requests the I-cache lines a few blocks ahead of the fetch PC, so fetch almost never waits on memory. What is this mechanism?
questions.explanation: Instruction prefetching (e.g., next-line or stream prefetchers) brings soon-needed code into cache ahead of the fetch PC, hiding instruction-miss latency.

questions.question: A compiler marks a loop's backward branch 'likely taken' with a hint bit, and the CPU obeys that fixed hint every time rather than learning from past outcomes. What kind of branch prediction is this?
questions.explanation: Static prediction decides once at compile time — e.g., 'backward taken, forward not-taken' heuristics or explicit hint bits — unlike dynamic predictors that adapt at runtime.

questions.question: If 20% of instructions in a pipeline each cause a one-cycle stall, what is the effective CPI?
questions.explanation: Effective CPI = base CPI + stall contribution = 1 + (0.20 x 1) = 1.2.

questions.question: A 4-stage pipeline has 2 ns stages plus 0.5 ns of latch overhead, while the equivalent non-pipelined delay is 8 ns. What is the speedup for a large number of instructions?
questions.explanation: The pipelined clock cycle is 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 ns, so speedup approaches 8 / 2.5 = 3.2, below the ideal of 4 due to latch overhead.

questions.question: In a 5-stage pipeline where branches resolve in the Execute stage, how many cycles are lost on each taken-branch misprediction?
questions.explanation: When the branch resolves in stage 3 (EX), the two instructions fetched into IF and ID are wrong-path and must be flushed, costing 2 cycles.

questions.question: In a classic 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding, how many stall cycles does a load-use data hazard require?
questions.explanation: A load produces its value only at the end of MEM, so the dependent instruction must stall one cycle before the value can be forwarded.

questions.question: A processor with an effective CPI of 1.25 executes 1 billion instructions on a 2 GHz clock. What is the execution time in seconds?
questions.explanation: Execution time = (instruction count x CPI) / clock rate = (10^9 x 1.25) / (2 x 10^9) = 0.625 seconds.

questions.question: A non-pipelined processor takes 20 ns per instruction. Its pipelined version uses 5 stages of 3 ns each plus 2 ns of latch overhead. What is the speedup for a very long instruction stream?
questions.explanation: Pipelined cycle = 3 + 2 = 5 ns; throughput speedup = 20 / 5 = 4, below the ideal 5 because of latch overhead.

questions.question: A 5-stage pipeline with no stalls executes 100 instructions. How many total clock cycles elapse from the first fetch to the last write-back?
Branches are 20% of instructions, 25% of branches are mispredicted, and each misprediction costs 2 cycles. What is the effective CPI?
An ideal 5-stage pipeline runs at 1 GHz and executes 200 instructions. What is the total elapsed time in nanoseconds?
questions.explanation: Cycles = 5 + 199 = 204; at 1 ns per cycle, elapsed time = 204 ns.

questions.question: A processor uses a single memory port shared by instruction fetch (IF) and data access (MEM), forcing a stall whenever both need it. Which hazard class is this?
questions.explanation: Structural hazards arise when hardware resources cannot support all simultaneous stage activities, e.g., one memory port for fetch and data.
